items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: There was Joe Thomas who played with Jimmie Lunceford, he was from Columbus, OH.

ctx.x: Every city seems to have had some legendary figures, some great musicians who never left or never made it who are always recalled with great affection and admiration by people who knew them but were as good as the people we later go to know but for one reason or another circumstances prevented them from either leaving or making it. Were there any local legends like that you might tell us about?

Columbus? There was Joe Thomas who played with Jimmie Lunceford, he was from Columbus, OH. Sy Oliver, he stayed around Columbus, OH for years but his home was right outside of Columbus, OH. Not Youngstown, that’s too far. But he’s a Buckeye—everybody from Ohio they’re called Buckeyes—but he stayed around Columbus for years. Nancy Wilson is from Columbus, OH.
These are all people that made it. Were there any that were great musicians but for one reason or another never left?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: And I remember once we had done so many one-nighters and Jimmy Lunceford, you know, he had such a disciplined band.

ctx.x: But he always says it. You know, when I'm trying to sort of define swing or something, he's always said, 'Oh, yeah, you know, people say this and that about it.' But he says, 'When they got in their thing, they could rock all night. It's different, an entirely different kind of band.

Yeah. But you know, they used to have a battle of the bands quite often, you know. And I remember once we had done so many one-nighters and Jimmy Lunceford, you know, he had such a disciplined band. They were all -- he was in the Cotton Club, you know. We never did have a chance to play in the Cotton Club, that nightclub. The only thing we did, Stanley, we'd do the Savoy sometimes for three weeks.
Were you in there when they went to the Grand Terrace?
